impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's anti-CGRP antibody patents, reinstating a jury verdict that Eli Lilly willfully infringed the patents covering methods of treating headache with humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. This case involves blockbuster migraine drug patents (Teva's Ajovy vs. Lilly's competing product) and has major implications for the scope of written description and enablement requirements for biologic drug patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biopharmaceutical innovators by affirming that genus claims to humanized antibodies can satisfy written description and enablement requirements even when only one specific antibody is disclosed, provided sufficient prior art methods of making such antibodies existed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar companies face greater barriers to invalidating broad biologic patent claims, potentially extending market exclusivity periods for branded biologic drugs and delaying lower-cost alternatives.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions using an emulator and function-call model are abstract and ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether damages for patent infringement may be based on foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict against Norton (Gen Digital), holding that Columbia's cybersecurity patents claiming methods for detecting anomalous program executions were directed to abstract ideas at Alice step one and required further step-two analysis on remand. The court also ruled that the district court erred in allowing damages based on Norton's foreign sales, reinforcing the territorial limits of U.S. patent law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies benefit from strengthened § 101 eligibility defenses against software patent claims, and the foreign sales damages ruling protects companies from U.S. patent damages liability for overseas revenue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the cybersecurity and software space face heightened risk that their claims will be deemed abstract under Alice, and cannot recover damages based on the infringer's foreign sales absent a sufficient domestic nexus.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights possesses sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain exclusionary rights—including the right to sue third parties for infringement—maintain sufficient Article III standing even after granting an exclusive license. The court found that retained rights to control sublicensing, assignment, and infringement litigation prevented the license from being a de facto assignment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring exclusive licenses can preserve standing to enforce their patents by retaining meaningful exclusionary rights such as the right to bring infringement suits, providing clarity for patent licensing and enforcement strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face reduced ability to challenge standing when patent owners retain enforcement rights in licensing agreements, narrowing a common early-stage defense in patent litigation.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support a jury finding that the plaintiff's asserted information constituted protectable trade secrets under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's trade secret misappropriation verdict, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying ideas were generally known. The court also reversed the patent invalidity finding for the same reason—the plaintiff's contribution of generally known ideas could not constitute an inventive contribution for inventorship correction. The counterfeiting verdict and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides important clarity that businesses cannot claim trade secret protection over information that is generally known in the industry, protecting companies from overbroad trade secret claims by competitors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret claims must ensure the asserted secrets are not generally known, or risk losing both trade secret protection and any derivative patent inventorship claims.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact precluded summary judgment on inequitable conduct in patent prosecution and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim alleging attempted monopolization through a fraudulently obtained patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgments on both inequitable conduct and Walker Process fraud claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact in both instances. The case involves allegations that Tenaris withheld prior art (the CYMAX Documents) during patent prosecution for coiled tubing patents and then used those patents to attempt to monopolize the market. The remand allows both the inequitable conduct defense and the antitrust counterclaim to proceed to trial.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of inequitable conduct benefit from the court's recognition that factual disputes about intent and materiality must go to trial rather than being resolved on summary judgment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who acquired prior art through asset purchases face heightened litigation risk if they fail to disclose those materials during prosecution, as competitors may pursue both inequitable conduct defenses and Walker Process antitrust claims.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and the doctrine of equivalents, and whether it properly struck a damages expert's theories for insufficient disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed-in-part and affirmed-in-part in a multicore processor patent dispute. The court reversed the extraterritoriality-based noninfringement ruling, holding that genuine fact issues existed about whether the claimed method was performed domestically. However, the court affirmed summary judgment on the doctrine of equivalents theory and the striking of certain damages expert theories for failure to disclose them in damages contentions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a more permissive approach to domestic infringement allegations for methods performed across international boundaries, expanding enforcement possibilities against global technology companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with distributed computing operations face increased patent infringement risk domestically, and the affirmance of striking inadequately disclosed damages theories reinforces strict compliance requirements for expert disclosures.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a split decision on eligibility, vacating summary judgment of eligibility for certain constellation design patents while affirming eligibility for others, based on whether the claims recited specific technical implementations or merely abstract mathematical optimization. The court affirmed the infringement and damages findings, including the admission of Constellation's damages expert testimony.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations in communications standards benefit from the court's affirmance of eligibility, and the damages ruling supports expert testimony methodologies in standards-essential patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing telecommunications standards face continued patent infringement liability for standard-essential patents, though claims directed purely to mathematical optimization may be vulnerable to § 101 challenges.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after having missed the statutory deadline to seek a stay in a previously filed declaratory judgment action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay under § 1659(a) by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. BioMarin had missed the 30-day window to seek a stay of Ascendis's original DJ action, then tried to obtain a mandatory stay after Ascendis refiled. The court closed this procedural loophole to prevent gamesmanship.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners pursuing ITC investigations benefit from the ruling preventing respondents from manipulating district court filings to obtain mandatory stays after missing statutory deadlines, preserving the ability to proceed in parallel forums.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day stay deadline cannot reset the clock through procedural maneuvering, requiring strict compliance with § 1659(a) timing requirements to obtain a mandatory stay of parallel district court litigation.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge, and whether the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires sales to expressly disclose the prior art device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the pre-AIA on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible regardless of the witness's personal knowledge and that the on-sale bar does not require that a prior art sale expressly disclose the sold device's internal functionality. The court also held that source code is not hearsay when offered to show computer commands rather than assertions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from broader admissibility of 30(b)(6) testimony in invalidity challenges and from the principle that prior commercial sales of a device invalidate later patents regardless of whether the sale disclosed internal functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased invalidity risk from prior commercial sales of embodying products, even where the prior sale did not reveal the inventive aspects of the technology, and cannot exclude corporate deposition testimony simply because the designated witness joined the company after the relevant events.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 by infringing Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of Apple Watch models incorporating blood oxygen functionality covered by Masimo's patents. The court found no error in the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings regarding wearable physiological measurement technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the medical device and wearable technology space are reinforced in their ability to use ITC proceedings to obtain exclusion orders against major technology companies importing infringing products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies incorporating health-monitoring features into consumer electronics face significant import exclusion risks from ITC proceedings brought by medical device patent holders, potentially requiring product redesigns or feature removal.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents should be interpreted as measured at a temperature standard in the field, and whether the patent holder was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents by Mylan's generic drug, agreeing that the pH claim limitation must be measured at the field-standard temperature (25°C) and that Actelion failed to prove infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. This decision clears the path for Mylan's generic version of Actelion's hypertension drug Veletri.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from clear claim construction principles requiring pH measurements at standard temperatures, facilitating design-around strategies and ANDA filings for generic drugs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies face narrower patent scope when claims reference measurable physical parameters, as courts will apply field-standard measurement conditions rather than conditions that might favor a broader infringement reading.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, including the reasonableness of attorneys' fees and the propriety of incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary exceeded its statutory authority by using PACER fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations. The court upheld the settlement terms, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, noting that hundreds of thousands of PACER users will be fully or substantially reimbursed.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement provides substantial reimbursement to businesses, law firms, and other entities that frequently access court records through PACER, and the ruling upholds the validity of incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives.
impacts.negativeImplications: The federal judiciary faces constraints on using PACER fees to fund unrelated technology projects, potentially requiring alternative funding sources for court technology initiatives that businesses benefit from.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a third party that was not sued for patent infringement but filed IPR petitions on the same day as the statutory deadline for the sued party may maintain IPR proceedings, and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination regarding FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent, finding insufficient support for the Board's analysis of dependent claims requiring reporting sensor information after a 'predetermined time delay.' The court declined to review the challenge to the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR, leaving open questions about third-party IPR petitions filed to assist sued parties.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from closer judicial scrutiny of Board obviousness determinations, particularly where dependent claim limitations are not adequately addressed in the prior art analysis.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies using third-party IPR petitions as a litigation strategy face uncertainty, and the vacatur signals that the Board must more rigorously analyze each claim limitation in obviousness determinations.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion by excluding a patent damages expert's report and granting summary judgment of no remedy based on that exclusion.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in a patent case against Microsoft's Azure SmartNIC technology, finding the district court applied an overly restrictive standard. The court vacated the resulting summary judgment based on absence of remedy and the denial of Exafer's motion to reopen discovery, remanding for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from a more permissive standard for admitting damages expert testimony, reducing the risk that technical deficiencies in expert reports will result in case-dispositive exclusions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Large technology companies like Microsoft face reduced ability to obtain summary judgment through Daubert challenges to damages experts, potentially increasing patent litigation exposure and settlement pressure.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly determined that Tineco's redesigned wet-dry surface cleaning devices did not infringe Bissell's patents, and whether the ITC correctly found Bissell established a technical domestic industry.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's Final Determination in full, upholding both the exclusion order for Tineco's original infringing products and the finding that Tineco's redesigned products did not infringe. The court also affirmed that Bissell satisfied the technical domestic industry requirement. This case illustrates the effectiveness of product redesigns in avoiding ITC exclusion orders.
impacts.positiveImplications: Importers and manufacturers benefit from confirmation that effective product redesigns can avoid ITC exclusion orders, providing a clear path to resume trade after an adverse ITC determination.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic patent holders may find ITC relief limited in duration if respondents can successfully redesign around the asserted patents, reducing the practical impact of exclusion orders.
